“Where does the beauty come to the world from? Where does it go? Or maybe it’s just hiding its face from us for a while?” 

The Wishing Tree (1977), directed by Tengiz Abuladze, is built around the tragic love story of Marita and Gedia. Marita is seen as pure, kind, and incredibly beautiful, someone the whole village admires and tries to “protect.” But that protection turns into control when the villagers, led by the powerful elder Tsitsikore, force her to marry a wealthy but cold man, believing she shouldn’t live in poverty. The problem is, her heart already belongs to Gedia.

But the film isn’t just a love story. It’s deeper and more symbolic. Abuladze fills it with hidden meanings about society, tradition, and control, especially reflecting the time it was made, during the Soviet era. Many of these ideas are subtle, almost hidden in the visuals and small details.

The movie opens with a striking scene of Gedia’s exhausted white horse dying in a field of red poppies. It feels symbolic, like the loss of freedom and innocence. The horse, often a symbol of purity and strength, can be seen as something bigger, even representing youth or the country itself, being slowly destroyed by those in power.

Throughout the film, Tsitsikore acts like an unchosen ruler, controlling people’s lives and decisions. Anyone who thinks differently is mocked or pushed aside, even though those “outsiders” are actually the most free-minded. Characters like Ioram challenge the system, speaking about progress and change, while others, like Fufala, live in their own world, showing both loneliness and quiet dignity.

As the story builds, it becomes clear that the real conflict isn’t just between people, but between freedom and control. The village, bound by fear, ignorance, and tradition, turns into a crowd that can easily destroy one of its own.

In the end, The Wishing Tree feels like a warning. It shows how dangerous it is when people stop thinking for themselves and blindly follow others. What happens to Marita isn’t just personal, it’s a reflection of a society that sacrifices beauty, love, and innocence without even realizing it.
